95: pH 4.5–5; about sixty acid hydrolases. This is where endocytosed LDL ends up: acid lipase hydrolyses its cholesteryl esters, NPC2 then NPC1 export the free cholesterol. Breakdown of lipid droplets (lipophagy) and of glycogen (acid α-glucosidase, deficient in Pompe disease).
96: Two perpendicular centrioles (9 microtubule triplets, ≈ 0.2 × 0.45 µm) in a pericentriolar material where γ-tubulin rings nucleate microtubules. In the hepatocyte it sits with the Golgi on the bile canaliculus side, towards which bile transporters are conveyed.
98: ESCRT complexes bud ≈ 50 nm vesicles inwards, loaded with receptors to be eliminated. It fuses with a lysosome, or with the plasma membrane, releasing exosomes.
100: β granules of 20–30 nm (up to ≈ 55,000 glucoses around one glycogenin) assembled into 100–200 nm α rosettes, specific to the liver. α-1,4 chains branched in α-1,6 every 8 to 12 residues. After a meal the liver stores up to ≈ 100 g; when fasting, phosphorylase then glucose-6-phosphatase return glucose to the blood: the liver maintains blood glucose. Insulin orders storage, glucagon and adrenaline order mobilisation.
102: A core of triglycerides and cholesteryl esters under a phospholipid monolayer studded with perilipins (PLIN2). It is born from the ER. A reserve mobilised by lipolysis and lipophagy, for β-oxidation or VLDL assembly. Their accumulation defines steatosis; the PNPLA3 p.Ile148Met variant is its main genetic factor.
103: You arrive with the blood in a cortical capillary. Its wall is tight: reach the golden rings ◎ and cross by transcytosis, then make for the synaptic bouton, where other rings mark the entrance. The “Take me to the entrance” button does the trip for you.
104: You are now in the synaptic bouton. Travel up the axon (22 µm) to the soma, like a signalling endosome hauled by dynein. Enlarge the ship (+), but not too much: the axon is only 0.8 µm wide.
105: Binding to TrkB: the ship passes itself off as a BDNF dimer, the neurotrophin released by the target neuron.
106: The two TrkB brought together phosphorylate each other on tyrosines (Ras–ERK, PI3K–Akt, PLCγ pathways); AP-2 and clathrin internalise the active complex.
107: Signalling endosome: TrkB stays active in the endosome membrane (Rab5, then Rab7). Dynein hauls it towards the soma along microtubules at ≈ 1–2 µm/s. On arrival, the ERK pathway (via the kinases RSK and MSK) leads to CREB phosphorylation: survival genes… and FOS.
109: You are against a synaptic bouton, a swelling on a collateral of this pyramidal neuron's axon. Opposite, across a 20 nm cleft, the dendritic spine of another neuron. Extracellular space takes up only ≈ 20 % of the tissue volume; astrocyte processes (not drawn) wrap the synapse and take glutamate back up. The small pairs of beads are BDNF dimers.
111: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP) and potassium leak channels set the resting potential, ≈ −70 mV. Voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels propagate the action potential. The membrane of the soma and dendrites receives thousands of synapses.
113: Receptor tyrosine kinase (gene NTRK2): leucine-rich and immunoglobulin domains outside, kinase inside. BDNF, a 27 kDa dimer, brings two TrkB together and they phosphorylate each other: Ras–ERK, PI3K–Akt and PLCγ pathways, for survival, dendrite growth and long-term potentiation. Land on the flagged pit (size ≤ 30 nm).
114: The activated BDNF–TrkB complex is internalised by AP-2 and clathrin. At the bouton, the same pits also recycle synaptic vesicle membrane after exocytosis.
116: The neuron's synthesis centre: almost all proteins of the axon, which has no rough ER, are made here and shipped out. The clusters of cisternae and polysomes are the Nissl bodies. The soma sums the signals coming from the dendrites; the action potential starts at the axon initial segment. Avoid the organelles!
118: Rosettes of free ribosomes between rough ER cisternae: this is the basophilia of Nissl bodies. They produce proteins of the cytosol and cytoskeleton (tubulin, neurofilaments), shipped down the axon by slow transport (0.2 to 8 mm per day).
120: Stacks of parallel cisternae in the soma and the base of dendrites, absent from the axon. Synthesis of membrane and secreted proteins: ion channels, receptors, pumps, synaptic vesicle proteins, neurotrophins. They disperse after axon section (chromatolysis).
121: A continuous network from the soma to the boutons and spines (spine apparatus). A Ca²⁺ store mobilised by IP₃ and ryanodine receptors; synthesis of membrane lipids.
122: A vast crown-shaped network around the nucleus, extended into the apical dendrite by Golgi outposts. It glycosylates and sorts proteins towards the axon (vesicles hauled by kinesins) or towards the dendrites.
123: The brain uses ≈ 20 % of the body's oxygen, mostly to restore ion gradients (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) after synaptic and action potentials. Mitochondria also buffer Ca²⁺. They are carried along microtubules (Miro and TRAK adaptors, kinesin-1, dynein) and stop where calcium rises, notably at synapses. Mitochondrial DNA of 16,569 bp (yellow dots).
124: A hollow 25 nm tube: 13 protofilaments of α/β-tubulin dimers. In the mature neuron they are no longer anchored to the centrosome. In the axon they all point their + end towards the terminal, stabilised by tau protein; in dendrites both orientations coexist (MAP2). Tracks for fast transport: kinesins towards the + end, dynein towards the − end.
126: Fast axonal transport: 50 to 400 mm per day (≈ 0.5–5 µm/s). Towards the terminal (kinesins): synaptic vesicle precursors, channels, mitochondria. Towards the soma (dynein): signalling endosomes carrying active TrkB, autophagosomes, material to be degraded.
127: Two centrioles near the nucleus. The neuron no longer divides and its centrosome no longer organises microtubules: they are nucleated locally in the soma, axon and dendrites.
128: pH 4.5–5, acid hydrolases. Concentrated in the soma: worn-out material from the terminals comes back here by retrograde transport. A neuron must last a lifetime; lysosomal defects weigh heavily on it (storage diseases, GBA1-linked forms of Parkinson's disease).
129: ESCRT complexes bud ≈ 50 nm vesicles inwards, loaded with receptors to be eliminated. Signalling endosomes coming from the axon end up here, then in the lysosome.
130: Wear-and-tear pigment: undigestible lysosomal residues (oxidised lipids and proteins) that build up with age in neurons, cells that do not divide.
131: 10 nm intermediate filaments (NF-L, NF-M, NF-H chains, α-internexin). Their phosphorylated side arms space them out and set the calibre of the axon, hence its conduction velocity. Blood NF-L level is used as a marker of axonal injury.
133: Trigger zone of the action potential: high density of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (Nav1.6, Nav1.2; red beads) and K⁺ channels (Kv7), anchored by ankyrin G to βIV spectrin. Under the membrane, actin rings spaced ≈ 190 nm apart by spectrin tetramers (pale hoops). A diffusion barrier that preserves the identity of the axon. Bundles of microtubules and neurofilaments at the centre.
